description: We are NULL GRAVITY, a team of five ambitious students from the Technical University of Cluj-Napoca (UTCN), brought together by our passion for technology, innovation, and space exploration. Our mission? To prove that while gravity might be missing, creativity and determination definitely aren't! For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are taking on the Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions challenge.
summary:
Orbital Health Console is an interactive prototype that helps astronauts monitor crew health and coordinate responses to medical concerns during space missions. We developed a web application combining individual health profiles, an interactive 3D body map, live simulated vital signs, medical records, and visual and spoken critical alerts.

The project addresses the challenge of astronaut health monitoring by bringing scattered information into one interface. It compares readings with personal baselines, flags outdated sensor data, and supports incident reporting and medical handovers. An offline-capable assistant helps users explore recorded information and reference protocols, while a station view connects crew health with repair-team planning.

Our prototype combines anonymized NASA Open Science Data Repository laboratory results with clearly identified simulated crew data. It demonstrates how accessible, locally available information could support crew autonomy when communication with Earth is limited.

This matters because recognizing changes and communicating clearly can help crews respond more effectively. The system supports human decision-making; it is not a validated medical device.
details:
Orbital Health Console is a prototype designed to help astronauts monitor crew health and coordinate responses to medical concerns during space missions. It brings health information, incident reporting, and station operations into one interactive interface.

The project’s source code is available on GitHub: Health Monitoring System — NASA Hackathon. (https://github.com/RusuAle/Health-Monitoring-System-NASA-Hackathon)

Each crew member has a profile containing vital signs, medical history, laboratory results, and health trends. An interactive 3D astronaut model allows users to select a body region and explore related findings, measurements, and reference protocols. The backend evaluates incoming data, compares measurements with personal baselines, detects outdated readings, and sends live updates to connected screens.

When a critical condition is detected, the application displays a prominent visual alert and can announce the astronaut’s name and the problem aloud. Crew members can acknowledge the alert, record observations, and request the medical officer. If the condition remains critical after the configured re-check period, the system raises the alert again. A shared timeline preserves these actions and supports medical handovers.

The project also includes an offline-capable assistant that helps users explore recorded information and reference protocols. It is designed to decline requests for diagnoses, medications, or doses. A station view connects crew health with operational planning by suggesting repair teams based on skills and current health assessments.

Our intended impact is to make important information easier to find, reduce the effort needed to interpret scattered records, and support clearer communication when access to ground-based assistance is limited. The prototype demonstrates how a locally running system could support greater crew autonomy while keeping medical decisions with qualified personnel.

We developed the application using JavaScript, TypeScript, React, and CSS, with Vite for frontend development. Three.js and React Three Fiber power the interactive 3D views. The backend uses Node.js and Express, with Server-Sent Events for live updates and a local event store for persistent records. The project includes Vitest unit tests and Playwright end-to-end tests. Local language-model integration is supported through Ollama, with a deterministic fallback when a model is unavailable. The application can run on a Windows computer.

Our data approach combines anonymized laboratory results from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository with fictional crew profiles and simulated vital signs informed by published spaceflight research. Real reference data, simulated measurements, and demonstration protocols are identified separately. Smartwatch integration is a planned extension; the current prototype does not yet receive live wearable data.

The project’s creativity lies in connecting an interactive body map, personal health trends, spoken alerts, incident coordination, and health-aware task planning. Rather than presenting measurements alone, it places them in the context of a crew member and the mission.

Throughout development, we considered limited connectivity, stressful operating conditions, individual differences, missing sensor data, traceability, and the need to distinguish evidence from simulation. The current system is a demonstration prototype, not a validated medical device. Clinical validation, secure authentication, privacy protections, and testing with real sensors are necessary before operational use.
